subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Permanent and induced magnetism, magnetic fields

questions.q: Which of these materials is magnetic?
questions.explain: Iron, along with steel, cobalt and nickel, is a magnetic material that is attracted to magnets.

questions.q: Outside a bar magnet, in which direction do the magnetic field lines point?
options: From north pole to south pole
From south pole to north pole
questions.explain: By convention, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet.

questions.q: What best describes an induced magnet?
options: A magnet that always keeps its magnetism
A material that becomes magnetic only when placed in a magnetic field
A magnet made only from copper
A magnet that produces its own permanent field
questions.explain: An induced magnet becomes magnetic in a field and largely loses this magnetism when removed from it.

questions.q: What happens when two like magnetic poles are brought close together?
questions.explain: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

questions.q: Where is the magnetic field of a bar magnet strongest?
questions.explain: The field is strongest at the poles, shown by the field lines being closest together there.

questions.q: A plotting compass placed in a room away from magnets points roughly north. What does this show?
options: The Earth has a magnetic field
questions.explain: A compass needle is a small magnet that aligns with the Earth's magnetic field, evidence the core is magnetic.

questions.q: What shape is the magnetic field produced around a straight current-carrying wire?
options: A field like a bar magnet
questions.explain: A current in a straight wire creates a field of concentric circles around it.

questions.q: The magnetic field pattern of a current-carrying solenoid most closely resembles that of which object?
questions.explain: A solenoid produces a uniform field inside and an external field like that of a bar magnet.

questions.q: Which equation gives the force on a conductor carrying a current at right angles to a magnetic field?
questions.explain: Force equals magnetic flux density multiplied by current multiplied by length of conductor in the field.

questions.q: What is the unit of magnetic flux density?
questions.explain: Magnetic flux density B is measured in tesla (T).

questions.q: A wire of length 0.10 m carries a current of 2.0 A at right angles to a field of flux density 0.50 T. What is the force on the wire?
In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the thumb represent?
questions.explain: Thumb is force/motion, first finger is field, second finger is current.

questions.q: Which change would reverse the direction of the force on a wire in an electric motor?
options: Reversing the direction of the current
Increasing the length of the wire
questions.explain: Reversing either the current or the field direction reverses the direction of the force.

questions.q: A 0.20 m length of wire experiences a force of 0.60 N in a field of flux density 1.5 T. What current flows in the wire?
questions.explain: Rearranging F = BIL gives I = F / (BL) = 0.60 / (1.5 x 0.20) = 2.0 A.

questions.q: How can a potential difference be induced in a coil of wire?
options: By moving a magnet into or out of the coil
By leaving a magnet still inside the coil
questions.explain: A changing magnetic field through the coil, produced by relative movement, induces a potential difference.

questions.q: A magnet is held stationary inside a coil connected to a sensitive meter. What is the induced potential difference?
questions.explain: No potential difference is induced without a changing magnetic field, so a stationary magnet gives zero.

questions.q: Which type of electrical supply must be used for a transformer to work?
questions.explain: Transformers need a continually changing (alternating) current to produce a changing magnetic field.

questions.q: Which equation relates the potential differences and turns of a transformer?
options: Vp x Vs = Np x Ns
questions.explain: The ratio of primary to secondary potential difference equals the ratio of primary to secondary turns.

questions.q: How is a step-up transformer constructed?
options: More turns on the primary than the secondary coil
More turns on the secondary than the primary coil
No turns on the secondary coil
questions.explain: A step-up transformer has more secondary turns, so the output potential difference is greater than the input.

questions.q: A transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 400 turns on the secondary. If the primary potential difference is 12 V, what is the secondary potential difference?
Why does the National Grid use step-up transformers to transmit electricity at high voltage?
options: To reduce power lost as heat in the cables
questions.explain: Higher voltage means lower current, which greatly reduces energy wasted as heat in the transmission lines.

questions.q: A 100% efficient transformer has a primary of 230 V, 2.0 A and a secondary of 23 V. What is the secondary current?
questions.explain: For 100% efficiency Vp Ip = Vs Is, so Is = (230 x 2.0) / 23 = 20 A.
